title: Kamarajar and the Village Panchayat: Democratic Decentralization and Rural Empowerment
summary: When introducing democratic Panchayat Raj legislation in Tamil Nadu, Chief Minister K. Kamaraj insisted that direct administrative and financial power must rest with village councils.
full_text:
In 1958, a high-level consultative conference was convened in the Chief Minister's secretariat at Fort St. George to draft the landmark Madras Panchayats Act.

Senior civil servants urged caution, arguing against transferring substantial financial powers and development budgets directly to elected village councils:
"Sir, rural villagers lack administrative sophistication and fiscal experience. If extensive spending authority is devolved to village panchayats, funds may be mismanaged. The District Collector must retain absolute supervisory control and veto power."

Chief Minister K. Kamaraj listened patiently, leaned forward, and addressed the bureaucrats with sharp common sense:
"I struggle to follow your logic. You trust the illiterate village peasant to cast his vote to elect members of parliament, legislators, and prime ministers. Yet you claim he lacks the intelligence to decide where to dig a drinking well or repair a village cart track?"

The room fell silent. Kamaraj continued with deep conviction:
"Bureaucracy must shed the illusion that wisdom resides only in air-conditioned secretariats. The farmer in the field knows the contours of the local irrigation tank far better than any visiting officer from the capital! They may make mistakes initially, but human beings learn responsibility only by exercising responsibility.
Do not hoard power in Chennai! Decentralize authority to the grassroots, for genuine democracy is born only when the village governs itself!"

Under Kamaraj’s decisive leadership, the 1958 Madras Panchayats Act became a pioneering national benchmark for democratic decentralization.
